name: Evidence-only household — J. Garland
head: inf_cooper_north_04

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints him at the Democrat of 11 June 1834, column 11, so he is in the town's paper by 1834-06-11 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when he came. The household used to carry the scene date as its bound, because nothing dated a hypothesised household — this is the same claim made against evidence instead of against the date the town is being counted on. Last printed 1834-06-11.

arrival_year.note: DRAWN, NOT READ. The household's arrival block holds a BOUND — somebody was here by 1834-06-11 and no source says when they came — so the year is drawn from the arrival years the known layer records, truncated at that bound and renormalised. It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

basis.note: data/reconstruction/1835_town_model.json#arrival_and_origin.tables.arrival_year_of_the_known_layer, restricted to years at or before 1834.

replaceable_by.match: a dated source that says which year this household came to Chicago

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: DRAWN FROM A SURVIVORSHIP SAMPLE. No source says where this household came from. The region is drawn from the birthplaces of the seventy Old Settlers who registered an arrival at or before 1835 — a self-selected roll set down forty-four years later that over-represents the men who stayed and prospered, as the town model's own open questions say. It is the only origin distribution this project holds and this value is drawn from it, not measured.

replaceable_by.match: a source that says where this household came from

reason_for_coming.value: The carrying trade at the head of the lake
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as cooper, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

basis.note: arrival_fill.trade_reasons.the_carrying_trade — the head's recorded trade is evidence about this household, and the draw it answered is the reason the record will carry until a source states one.

replaceable_by.match: a source that says why this household came, or a committed source that apportions the town's arrivals between the land sales, the canal and the harbour works

lives_at.note: T-0489: former dwelling assignment came from the retired reconstructed-household programme; real resident retained unplaced.

works_at.note: T-0489: no workplace is assigned from a reconstructed household; later placement requires evidence.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: J. Garland

occupation.note: THE TRADE IS THE PAPER'S, NOT THE CENSUS'S. The corpus reads him as cooper, at the Democrat of 11 June 1834, column 11. This record used to carry the occupation census's argument for the trade instead — that a town of this size needs so many of them — which is why the household exists; it is no longer why this man holds the trade. Where the corpus prints more than one trade for him, they are all recorded here and the household's is the one the register matched.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED MAN ON A RECONSTRUCTED ROOF. The papers name him and this household's dwelling does not: what is attested is the person and his trade, and what remains the reconstruction's is everything about where he lived. He is printed as 'J. GARLAND' and the corpus reads his trade as cooper. Cited at the Democrat of 11 June 1834, column 11. THIS ROOF DID NOT COME FROM HIS RECORD. The household was raised by the occupation census because the town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings needed a cooper and no documented one was available; the register (data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json, action `replace_invented`) is what says one now is. The dwelling's existence, position and footprint are unchanged and still conjectural, and nothing here claims he slept in it — only that the town's need for this trade is met by a man the papers name rather than by one this project invented. The invented name this record used to carry, and its name_basis block, are retired: an invented name is not kept beside a documented one. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the placement is L205. He is placed nowhere in particular by his own record, which is the condition of taking ANY roof of his trade — a man the papers put on a named street takes only a roof the plat stands on that street (T-0367), and one they place somewhere this scene cannot honour is refused outright. READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

dated_bounds.identity_rule: data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json — persons[] person_j_garland, action `enrich` onto this card. The register states its own reason there and this row cites it rather than transcribing it.
dated_bounds.note: AN APPEARANCE IN THE TOWN'S PRINT, AND NOTHING FURTHER. The Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-11 names 'J. GARLAND' in the claim read as chicago_democrat_1834_06_11#c011, so the reading dates an appearance of this person in the town's press and `here_by` is null: a name in print is not a body in the town, and a notice can be signed elsewhere and reprinted here. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes, and a source LATER than it does not promote either. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT: the issue is deposited, dated and numbered in data/research/newspapers/corpus.json, and what no source states is that the name the paper prints is the person on this card — the register joins them under its own written note. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

PRINTED AGAINST THIS NAME IN THE 1833-1835 PRESS and carried here from the newspaper gazetteer (T-1254, by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). The gazetteer holds its trades on the PERSON record and not on a single issue, so the bound is the run of this person's own dated mentions, 1834-06-11 to 1834-06-11, and the grade is `inferred`: the paper printed the trade, and the resident programme's identity rule tied the printing to this card. The scene date falls outside that run, so this role does not stand in the 1835 view.

basis.note: Drawn at 85.7% male, the rate measured on the unclaimed roll's own people whose sex the evidence settles. data/reconstruction/1835_sex_age_model.json holds the measurement.

replaceable_by.match: a source that records this person's sex, a gendered title on their name, or a forename the project's evidence lets fire

sex_basis.note: A DRAW, NOT A READING. Nothing about this person says which sex they were: T-1303 refused the name and was right to. This value is drawn from the measured male share of the roll the person was named on, seeded by their own id so the draw reproduces - retype 'inf_cooper_north_04:sex_ratio' and the same face comes up. It carries no weight as evidence about this person and it is never promoted. The rate is a ceiling rather than a point reading, because the forename table that settled the rest was built mostly on men's names.

basis.note: Drawn from the 1840 Chicago schedule's column 'free white males 30 under 40', one of its male bands, conditioned on `civic_list_20_and_over` because the person stands on a poll, a tax list or a muster roll.

replaceable_by.match: a source that states this person's age, their birth year, or an interval either can be read out of

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('inf_cooper_north_04:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a poll, tax or muster list names a person 20 or over - the 1840 schedule's own adult line. THE FRANCHISE'S AGE RULE IS NOT IN ANY SOURCE RECORD THIS PROJECT HOLDS; this is the model's conditioning and not a reading (T-1303's finding, handed to T-1304). No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - fourth of 4 cooper households in this layer, in the north division. A TOWN PACKING THOUSANDS OF HOGS A SEASON NEEDS COOPERS, AND THIS DATASET HELD NONE. Andreas records that Clybourne packed some 250 head of cattle and about 2,000 hogs in the season of 1833, that George W. Dole packed a further 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs at the same place, and that the Newberry & Dole house on the South Branch packed 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in 1834 (scan p. 1151). Packed provisions travel in barrels and barrels are made by coopers. The documented layer holds a packer, two slaughter-houses and not one cooper. Four cooper households are inferred against the schedule's six W3 cooper, wagon or wheelwright shops. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one. RETIRED AN INVENTED NAME (T-0264). This household was raised by the occupation census and named from the invented-name pools. The newspaper register matched it to J. Garland, a documented cooper the corpus names 1 time(s) and places nowhere in particular, and he now holds the roof. What changed is WHO: the argument for the household, its dwelling and its position are untouched and still the reconstruction's, and the person's grade is `inferred` — a real man with reconstructed details — rather than `attested`, which would claim the dwelling too. tools/replace_invented_residents.py derives this deal and prints every candidate it refused. T-0489: reconstructed occupancy retired; evidence-based person retained and unplaced.
